prime.problem: A radix-tree cache lives in one GPU's HBM, which it shares with the running batch: at most 488k tokens of Llama-3.1-8B per H100. Kimi's long, repetitive traffic reuses far more KV than that, and moving KV between machines was assumed to need too much bandwidth.
prime.fits: First Mooncake card. RadixAttention reused KV within a GPU; Mooncake keeps it in a cluster-wide pool of CPU DRAM and SSD, and this card checks when loading a prefix beats recomputing it. Prefill/decode disaggregation from perf-2 is the setting.
expect: KV tiers: HBM → DRAM → SSD → remote DRAM
Mooncake Store: paged blocks, prefix-chained hash keys, replicas, LRU
capacity: 3M tokens per node vs 50M needed
prime.goal: Compute the minimum bandwidth for loading KV to beat recomputing it, and explain why a pooled cross-machine cache beats a local one.

attend: Loading a prefix costs bytes; recomputing it costs FLOPs. What ratio decides which is faster, and why does it barely depend on prefix length?
Why is the bandwidth bar lower for a bigger model and higher for a faster GPU?
Why is each block's hash key built from its own tokens and its prefix?
Why does one node's DRAM catch less than half of the reusable hits in the paper's traces?
Which tier does Mooncake add that a single-node engine doesn't have?

must: Recompute costs l(a p² d + b p d²) FLOPs → loading costs the prefix's KV bytes → load wins when bandwidth B > 2sG / (gqa·(a p + b d)) → only a few GB/s (6 for LLaMA3-70B on 8×A800, ≈ 9 for Llama-3.1-8B on H100) → cross-machine KV is cheap enough

One node's DRAM holds ~3M tokens of 70B KV → most reusable prefixes land on other nodes or get evicted → pool every node's DRAM and SSD into one store reachable over RDMA → hit rate up to +136%, prefill time up to −48% vs local caches

KV of a block depends on everything before it → key = hash(block, prefix) → identical prefixes deduplicate, same tokens after a different prefix don't collide → hot keys get replicas on many nodes so one NIC isn't a bottleneck
elevated: B_min scales with G (GPU FLOP/s) and falls as b·d and gqa grow → faster GPUs raise the bar (H800 needs ~3× the A800's) → future GPUs make storing harder, bigger models make it easier
reference: Transfer Engine internals (16 KB slices, NIC selection, endpoint pooling)
the paper's b = 22 vs our b = 26
exact Transfer Engine measurements (87 and 190 GB/s)
the prefill and decode pools' SLO thresholds

compress.prompt: From memory, write the store-vs-recompute inequality in words (bytes to load ÷ bandwidth < FLOPs to recompute ÷ compute), then the three things Mooncake Store does, then one line on why the pool must span machines.
checklist: load time = prefix KV bytes ÷ B; recompute time = prefill FLOPs ÷ G
B_min is a few GB/s and shrinks for bigger models
paged blocks with prefix-chained hash keys (dedup)
replicas for hot blocks, LRU eviction
one node's DRAM is too small to catch most repeats (Fig 9)

retrieve.q: Explain why moving KV between machines turned out to be affordable, contrary to the assumption other systems made.
answer: prefill is expensive per token, so recomputing a prefix costs many FLOPs per KV byte
the break-even bandwidth is only ~6 GB/s for LLaMA3-70B on 8×A800
a 100 Gbps NIC carries 12.5 GB/s, so RDMA networks clear the bar

retrieve.q: Walk through the four-step workflow for a request whose prefix is cached in the pool.
answer: s1: the prefill node loads the matching prefix blocks from remote DRAM into HBM
s2: it prefills only the uncached tail, chunked and pipelined if long; new KV goes back to CPU memory
s3: the store streams KV layer by layer to the chosen decode node, overlapped with s2
s4: the request joins that node's continuous batch

retrieve.q: When is keeping KV in a remote store a bad deal?
answer: slow links: below ~9.3 GB/s the 8B can lose to recompute; a 25 Gbps link loses even at 32k
short prefixes: savings of ~15 ms can be eaten by lookup, round trip and imperfect overlap
low reuse: in the arXiv trace over half of cached blocks were never used
fast GPUs raise the bandwidth bar

compare.q: RadixAttention caches prefixes in one GPU's HBM; Mooncake in a cluster DRAM/SSD pool. What is fundamentally traded, which design choice makes each fast, and how does each fail?
answer: HBM: 3.35 TB/s, no transfer cost, but capacity shared with the batch (≤ 488k tokens of the 8B)
pool: terabytes to petabytes, but every hit costs a network transfer
radix fails by evicting under batch pressure; the pool fails when the link is below B_min or reuse is low

compare.q: Course 6 covers disaggregated prefill and decode (Splitwise, Mooncake, Dynamo). What does Mooncake's KV store add on top of disaggregation itself?
answer: disaggregation already moves each request's KV from prefill to decode nodes
Mooncake also keeps KV after the request, in a shared pool, and reuses it for later requests
the same RDMA path serves both transfer and reuse

predict.q: Llama-3.1-8B on one H100 with a 2,000-token cached system prompt. Is loading it over a 25 Gbps link (3.1 GB/s) faster than recomputing? Over 100 Gbps (12.5 GB/s)? Commit first.
predict.answer: The prefix is 2,000 × 128 KiB = 0.262 GB. Recompute by Eq 1 at 100% of 989 TF: about 30.3 ms. At 3.1 GB/s loading takes about 84 ms, so recompute wins; at 12.5 GB/s about 21 ms, so loading wins, but only by ~9 ms before any lookup or overlap overhead. B_min at p = 2,000 is 8.64 GB/s (our arithmetic with the card's a = 4, b = 26).

apply.task: Run labs/store-vs-recompute.py. Then compute by hand, for Llama-3.1-8B on an H100 at prefix p = 2,000: B_min, the KV size, the recompute time (Eq 1 at 100% of G) and the load time over 50 GB/s and 12.5 GB/s. Finally set G to 50% of 989 TF in the lab and say what happens to B_min and why.
apply.done: Your hand numbers match the lab's formula to three figures, and you can explain the 50%-G change in one sentence.
apply.hint: B_min = 2·2·989e12 / (4·(4·2,000 + 26·4,096)) = 8.64 GB/s; KV 0.262 GB; recompute 30.3 ms; load 5.2 ms at 50 GB/s and 21.0 ms at 12.5 GB/s (our arithmetic). Halving G halves B_min: a slower GPU makes recomputing costlier, so storing wins more easily.

Could you explain why B_min shrinks for bigger models, without the formula?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: GPU speed → B_min, or capacity per node → hit rate?
Did you distinguish FAST'25 numbers from the arXiv report's?
What will you look for in Mooncake II: how the scheduler decides where a request runs, now that KV can move?
